posts.body_html: Our experience with systemic fungicides on Sarracenia here in southern Florida: deformed pitchers, and when temps are high in summer, it can kill them.
posts.body_text: Our experience with systemic fungicides on Sarracenia here in southern Florida: deformed pitchers, and when temps are high in summer, it can kill them.

posts.body_html:
I would tend to agree that the topical fungicides usually work fine for Sarracenia rhizomes. We use sulfur fungicides such as those found in "Safer" brand products. Sulfur has a residual effect, so it works well as a preventative. I know it can cause problems in high temperatures, but like any of this stuff, you have to follow the label.

I have used Tebuconazole products many times since it's found in Bayer disease control concentrate that you have to mix, and in their 3 in 1 pre-mixed combination product. It's been mostly in our greenhouse for powdery mildew on Cephalotus. The concentrations in Bayer products are probably less than an agricultural product such as Merit. A couple cautions, however. The first is in using Ag chemicals unless you are really sure of your end product concentration. We've had some mishaps in the nursery with that. Also, you're dealing with a much more hazardous concentrate that most products made for home use. The other caution is on systemic fungicides themselves. We don't use in on Cephalotus anymore, and not because it harmed them, but it doesn't work anymore. Fungi build resistance to systemics relatively quickly. Topicals like Captan and Sulfur work more by making the environment inhospitable to the fungi.

One product that may be of consideration for battling fungal problems is Trichoderma. It's a predatory fungal spore product applied as a root drench. Here's an example of the product: www.territorialseed.com/product/130 Like anything it's probably best to try it on a few plants first to make sure it won't give any adverse results. We haven't used in on Sarracenia simply because we haven't needed to. I have used it on Cephalotus with good results.

Jeff

posts.body_html:
Hi Corey,

It is for general gardening supplies. Territorial is a good company, but you can probably find Root Shield at several gardening vendors. The one caution I didn't mention above about Trichoderma is that some sundews don't respond well to the stuff. I seem to recall reading somewhere that with their very tiny roots, the fungus tries to colonize, and if it doesn't have pathogenic fungi to feed on it becomes harmful to them. With bigger stockier plants such as Pitcher Plants, it behaves much more like a mycorrhizal fungi.

On a side note, Trichoderma is almost magical on fungal prone garden plants like tomatoes. If you haven't been able to rotate a crop due to space issues, this can really get you another season with them in the same place since it will keep Pythium and Rhizoctonia at bay.

Jeff

posts.body_html:
Good thread guys! I learn so much on here.
Went on my repotting and dividing spree today! After a 5 hour whirlwind it's all done (fortunately my collection isn't so large as to take multiple days of work, like Mike's!). No pics but they look tidy with all the brown trimmed away. I definitely leave the green alas of pitchers and phyllodia in place to permit photosynthesis. 
I broke down and put my plants back in their water trays. It's just been so darn warm that they've been drying out on me, especially smaller pots. I am paranoid about rot so I put them in only 1/2" or so of water so they stay moist but aren't waterlogged.
Definitely no Polar Vortex here: one of my flavas already has a flower bud showing. It's a rugelii and I would expect that southern plant to bloom early, but dang. Such a crazy "winter" - did all the work with my shirt off soaking up the rays!

posts.body_html: Everything I have is in growth, so today I went through the collection and did a second trimming. Fully cut off most of the old pitchers, many of which I had left only partially trimmed, and trimmed of any brown that had developed since my first trim in December. Phyllodia I left alone. Also went in and thinned the purps and roseas (especially my uber-weedy bazillion growth point montanas from Mike to make sure the growth points receive light. I'm going to do a third trimming once the plants have opened their first traps, probably in the next month depending on the plant.

posts.body_html:
joanne-totally missed your question, but fortunately, Calen dug up this thread The leaves furthest away from the dormant growth tip are completely taken off, even if they're green. Typically, this is 3-4 leaves maximum-I snap them off like you would snap off a petiole of celery (although it's 10X harder to do with Sarracenia). This exposes dormant "eyes" on the rhizome, and allows side shoots to form.

The rest of the traps that are green are left on-these are typically traps that were formed in late summer/early fall, so they're a lot "fresher" and can last a while. When you have 2-3 new pitchers in late spring/early summer, then those old leaves from the previous year can snapped off, although I leave them there throughout the season for the most part (too time consuming to go through the collection for a second trim). However, if you want to grow Sarracenias for Jesus, it's best to do the second round of trimming. So much easier to show with pictures-if you don't get it, let me know and I'll take some before and after pics to demonstrate.

Calen: green phyllodia and traps are equally valuable to the plant, even if there's new growth just starting. In fact, if you have an old trap that's still green and has old insects in it from last year, leave those on until around May (for us in California).

How do you know when to chop them off completely? When you have new pitchers catching a lot of insects, the plant no longer needs the old stuff. Keeping the old traps on is one of the "secrets" to producing gigantic traps on large rhizomes.

I say good move on the purps.-they don't have any space to grow, so they benefit from "thinning" this time of year if they were very dense the previous year.

Keep in mind these methods are over the top: you can technically trim everything off to the ground in december or during the dormancy period and still produce beautiful plants.

posts.body_html: Sorry Kimbruun, corrected the grammar.  What I'm saying is observations in the wild contradict observations in cultivation.  In other words, while there are consistent and measurable benefits to leaving traps on in cultivation, it may still be possible to produce giant traps in cultivation even if you cut off all the old growth.  I'm not sure how that is possible, but observations in the wild suggest it is.

posts.body_html: You had mentioned Mealy Bugs earlier as a challenge w warmer weather climates...  any recommendations on how to control them?  I just planted all my potted plants into a bog, and a few of the pots were just full of root mealy bugs.  I washed every bit of dirt I could off and removed all the old pitchers before replanting.
